title: Find Maximum Element in an Array
description:
Given an array of integers, find and return the largest element present in the array.

You need to solve the problem by traversing the array and comparing each element with the current maximum value.

examples.explanation: 8 is the largest element in the array.
-1 is the maximum value among all elements.
A single element array contains its own maximum value.

hints: Assume the first element is the maximum.
Traverse the array and compare each element.
Update the maximum whenever a larger value is found.
intuition: The maximum element can be found by checking every element once. Keep track of the largest value seen so far while traversing the array.

patternExplanation.name: Linear Array Traversal
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Visit every element once and maintain the required information.

bruteForce.reason: Every element needs to be checked once.

optimal.reason: Single traversal with one variable is enough.

approaches.name: Brute Force (Built-in Max)
Linear Traversal (Optimal)
Java Streams (Modern Approach)

edgeCases.reason: The only element is the maximum.
Maximum can still be a negative value.
Return the maximum value regardless of duplicates.

pitfalls: Initializing maximum as 0 because the array can contain negative values.
followUpQuestions: Find maximum and minimum together in one traversal.

notes.title: Basic Array Pattern
notes.description: Array traversal is the foundation for many advanced problems.

notes.title: Single Pass Optimization
notes.description: Always check if the answer can be maintained while traversing instead of using extra operations.

title: Find Minimum Element in an Array
description:
Given an array of integers, find and return the smallest element present in the array.

The solution should scan the array once and keep track of the minimum value found so far.

examples.explanation: 1 is the smallest element in the array.
-10 is the minimum value.

hints: Assume the first element is the minimum.
Compare every element with the current minimum.
Update the minimum whenever a smaller value is found.
intuition: Just like finding the maximum element, we can maintain a variable that stores the smallest value seen during traversal.

patternExplanation.name: Minimum Tracking
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Maintain the smallest value while visiting every array element once.

optimal.reason: Single traversal is enough.

approaches.name: Brute Force (Built-in Min)
Linear Traversal (Optimal)
Java Streams (Modern Approach)

edgeCases.reason: The only element is the minimum.
Minimum can be a negative number.

notes.title: Traversal Pattern
notes.description: Many array problems can be solved by maintaining a running answer.

title: Calculate Sum of All Elements in an Array
description: Given an integer array, calculate the sum of all elements present in the array.
hints: Create a variable to store the running sum.
Add every element while traversing the array.
intuition: Maintain a running total and add each element as you move through the array.

patternExplanation.name: Accumulator Pattern
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Keep updating a result variable while processing elements.

bruteForce.reason: Each element contributes to the final sum.

optimal.reason: Only one variable is required.

approaches.name: Brute Force (Index-based)
Enhanced For Loop (Optimal)
Java Streams (Modern Approach)

pitfalls: Using int when sum can exceed integer range.
followUpQuestions: Find sum of even and odd numbers separately.

notes.title: Accumulator Technique
notes.description: A common approach used in many array and string problems.

title: Reverse an Array Using Two Pointers
description:
Given an array of integers, reverse the array in-place without using extra space.

You need to modify the original array so that the first element becomes the last and the last element becomes the first.

examples.explanation: The array is reversed by swapping elements from both ends.
First and last elements are swapped, then the middle element remains unchanged.

hints: Use two pointers: one at the start and one at the end.
Swap values at both pointers.
Move both pointers towards the center.
intuition: The first element needs to move to the last position, and the last element needs to move to the first position. Two pointers allow us to swap matching positions from both ends until they meet.

patternExplanation.name: Opposite Direction Two Pointers
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Use two indexes moving towards each other to process elements from both ends.

bruteForce.reason: Create a new array and copy elements in reverse order.

optimal.reason: Swap elements inside the same array using two pointers.

approaches.name: Brute Force (Extra Array)
Two Pointer Approach (Optimal)
Built-in Method (Java)

edgeCases.reason: There are no elements to reverse.

followUpQuestions: Reverse only a part of an array.
Reverse a string using two pointers.
Check if an array is a palindrome.

notes.title: Two Pointer Foundation
notes.description: This is one of the most basic and important two pointer patterns.

notes.title: In-place Modification
notes.description: Two pointers often help reduce extra space usage.

title: Container With Most Water
description:
You are given an integer array height where height[i] represents the height of a vertical line at index i.

Find two lines that together with the x-axis form a container that can hold the maximum amount of water.

Return the maximum amount of water the container can store.

examples.explanation: The lines at index 1 and index 8 create the container with maximum area: min(8,7) * (8-1) = 49.
Only one possible container exists.

hints: Start with two pointers at both ends.
Area depends on the shorter line.
Move the pointer pointing to the smaller height.
intuition: The area of water depends on two things: the distance between lines and the shorter height. Starting from both ends gives maximum width. To improve the area, move the pointer with the smaller height because the shorter line limits the container.

patternExplanation.name: Opposite Direction Two Pointers
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Use two pointers from both ends and reduce the search space intelligently.

bruteForce.reason: Check every possible pair of lines.

optimal.reason: Each pointer moves only once across the array.

approaches.name: Brute Force
Two Pointer (Optimal)

edgeCases.reason: Maximum area depends only on width.
The shorter line still limits the area.

pitfalls: Moving the taller pointer instead of shorter one.
Calculating area using maximum height instead of minimum height.
followUpQuestions: Why do we move the smaller height pointer?
Can this problem be solved using dynamic programming?
How would you return the actual two indices?

notes.title: Greedy + Two Pointer
notes.description: The optimal solution works because we discard impossible smaller areas by moving the limiting pointer.

notes.title: Important Observation
notes.description: Area = minimum(height[left], height[right]) × distance between pointers.

title: Trapping Rain Water
description:
Given an elevation map represented by an integer array height where each element represents the height of a bar, calculate how much rainwater can be trapped after raining.

Each bar has width 1.

examples.explanation: The total trapped water between the bars is 6 units.
The trapped water between boundaries is 9 units.

hints: Water trapped at any index depends on the tallest bar on its left and right.
Use two pointers instead of storing leftMax and rightMax arrays.
Move the pointer with the smaller height.
intuition: For every position, trapped water is determined by the smaller boundary between the left maximum and right maximum. Instead of calculating left and right maximum arrays, maintain them while moving two pointers from both ends.

patternExplanation.name: Two Pointer Boundary Tracking
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Maintain left and right maximum boundaries while shrinking the search space.
whenToUse: Problems involving left and right boundaries

bruteForce.reason: For every index, find maximum height on left and right separately.

prefixArray.reason: Store left maximum and right maximum arrays.

optimal.reason: Calculate trapped water while moving two pointers.

approaches.name: Brute Force
Prefix/Suffix Arrays
Two Pointer (Optimal)

pitfalls: Using maximum height instead of minimum boundary.
Forgetting to update leftMax and rightMax.
followUpQuestions: Solve using prefix and suffix arrays.
Explain why moving the smaller pointer is correct.
Find the total trapped water using stack approach.
Can you solve it in one pass?

notes.title: Classic Two Pointer Problem
notes.description: This is one of the most important advanced two pointer problems.

notes.title: Space Optimization
notes.description: The prefix maximum approach uses O(n) space, while two pointers reduce it to O(1).

title: Valid Palindrome
description:
Given a string s, determine if it is a palindrome after converting all uppercase letters into lowercase letters and removing all non-alphanumeric characters.

A palindrome is a string that reads the same forward and backward.

examples.input: s = "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"
examples.explanation: After removing spaces and symbols: "amanaplanacanalpanama" which is a palindrome.
The cleaned string "raceacar" is not the same forward and backward.

hints: Use two pointers from both ends.
Ignore non-alphanumeric characters.
Compare lowercase characters.
intuition: A palindrome is symmetric, so we only need to compare characters from both ends. Two pointers allow checking the string without creating another reversed string.

patternExplanation.name: Opposite Direction Two Pointers
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Compare matching positions from the beginning and end.

bruteForce.reason: Create cleaned string and compare with reverse.

optimal.reason: Compare characters directly using two pointers.

approaches.name: Brute Force (String Builder)
Two Pointer (Optimal)

edgeCases.reason: An empty string is considered a palindrome.

notes.title: Two Pointer String Pattern
notes.description: Same logic as reversing an array, but applied to characters.

title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array
description:
Given an integer array nums sorted in non-decreasing order, remove duplicates in-place such that each unique element appears only once.

Return the number of unique elements.

examples.explanation: The modified array becomes [1,2,_].
Unique elements are [0,1,2,3,4].

hints: Array is already sorted.
Use one pointer for placing unique elements.
Use another pointer for scanning.
intuition: Because the array is sorted, duplicates are always next to each other. One pointer tracks where the next unique element should be placed while another scans the array.

patternExplanation.name: Slow and Fast Pointer
patternExplanation.coreIdea: One pointer reads values while another modifies the array.

bruteForce.reason: Use extra data structure to store unique elements.

optimal.reason: Modify the array in-place.

approaches.name: Brute Force (Extra Array)
Two Pointer (Optimal)

pitfalls: Not taking advantage of sorted property.
followUpQuestions: Move all zeroes to the end.

notes.title: Slow Fast Pointer
notes.description: One of the most common in-place array modification patterns.

title: Move Zeroes
description:
Given an integer array nums, move all 0's to the end of it while maintaining the relative order of the non-zero elements.

The operation must be done in-place without making a copy of the array.

examples.explanation: All non-zero elements are moved forward while zeros are shifted to the end.
Single zero remains unchanged.

hints: Use one pointer to track the position of the next non-zero element.
Scan the array using another pointer.
Swap non-zero elements forward.
intuition: We need to keep the order of non-zero elements and push zeros to the end. The fast pointer searches for non-zero values, while the slow pointer represents the position where the next non-zero value should be placed.

patternExplanation.name: Slow and Fast Pointer
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Use one pointer for reading values and another for placing valid values.

bruteForce.reason: Create another array and copy non-zero values.

optimal.reason: Modify the same array using pointers.

approaches.name: Brute Force (Extra Array)
Two Pointer Without Swap
Two Pointer Swap (Optimal)

followUpQuestions: Move all negative numbers to one side.
Move all even numbers before odd numbers.
Remove all occurrences of a given value.

notes.title: In-place Array Transformation
notes.description: This pattern appears frequently in interviews where extra space is restricted.

title: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
description:
Given a 1-indexed array of integers numbers that is already sorted in non-decreasing order, find two numbers such that they add up to a specific target number.

Return the indices of the two numbers.

examples.explanation: numbers[1] + numbers[2] = 2 + 7 = 9.
numbers[1] + numbers[3] = 2 + 4 = 6.

constraints: numbers is sorted in increasing order
hints: Because the array is sorted, use two pointers.
If sum is too small, move left pointer.
If sum is too large, move right pointer.
intuition: The sorted order gives us information. If the current sum is smaller than the target, increasing the left pointer increases the sum. If the sum is larger, decreasing the right pointer reduces the sum.

patternExplanation.name: Sorted Array Two Pointer
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Use ordering information to eliminate unnecessary searches.

optimal.reason: Two pointers scan the array once.

approaches.name: Brute Force
HashMap Approach
Two Pointer (Optimal)

pitfalls: Using HashMap when sorted property is available.
followUpQuestions: Solve Two Sum on unsorted array.
Find all pairs with given sum.

notes.title: Sorted Array Advantage
notes.description: Sorting enables eliminating half of the search space.

notes.title: Two Sum Foundation
notes.description: This pattern is the base for many k-Sum problems.

title: Squares of a Sorted Array
description: Given an integer array nums sorted in non-decreasing order, return an array of the squares of each number sorted in non-decreasing order.

examples.explanation: Squares are [16,1,0,9,100], which after sorting become [0,1,9,16,100].

constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: Largest square can come from either end.
Use two pointers at both ends.
Fill the result array from the end.
intuition: Negative numbers can become large after squaring. Since the array is sorted, the largest absolute values are always at the ends. Compare both ends and place the larger square at the end of the result array.

patternExplanation.name: Two Pointer From Both Ends
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Use sorted order to process the largest values first.

bruteForce.reason: Square all numbers then sort the result.

optimal.reason: Use two pointers and fill output directly.

approaches.name: Brute Force (Sort After Square)
Two Pointer (Optimal)

edgeCases.reason: Largest squares come from the left side.
Largest squares come from the right side.
Zero should appear at correct sorted position.

followUpQuestions: Can you solve it without extra space?
Why do we fill from the end?
How would this work for cubes?

notes.title: Sorted Array Pattern
notes.description: When data is sorted, two pointers can avoid extra sorting.

title: Backspace String Compare
description:
Given two strings s and t, return true if they are equal when both are typed into empty text editors.

'#' represents a backspace character.

examples.explanation: Both become "ac" after applying backspaces.
s becomes "c" while t remains "b".

constraints: s and t contain lowercase letters and '#'
hints: You can process strings from the end.
Skip characters removed by backspace.
Avoid building new strings.
intuition: Backspaces affect characters before them. Processing from the end allows us to skip deleted characters without modifying the string.

patternExplanation.name: Reverse Two Pointer
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Traverse from the end and ignore invalid characters.

optimal.reason: Compare characters directly from the end.

approaches.name: Two Pointer From End

edgeCases.reason: Deleted characters may change final length.

pitfalls: Processing from left without handling deletions.

notes.title: Reverse Traversal
notes.description: Some problems become easier when processed from the opposite direction.

title: 3Sum Closest
description:
Given an integer array nums and an integer target, find three integers in nums such that the sum is closest to target.

Return the sum of the three integers.

examples.explanation: The sum 2 is closest to target 1.
Only possible sum is 0.

hints: Sort the array first.
Fix one element and solve two sum closest.
Move pointers based on current sum.
intuition: After sorting, fix one number and use two pointers for the remaining two numbers. If the current sum is smaller than target, increase it by moving left. If larger, decrease it by moving right.

patternExplanation.name: Sorted Two Pointer Search
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Convert three element search into one fixed element plus a two pointer scan.

optimal.reason: Sorting plus two pointer traversal.

approaches.name: Sorting + Two Pointer

edgeCases.reason: Pointer movement still works after sorting.

followUpQuestions: Find k numbers closest to target.
Count triplets with sum smaller than target.

notes.title: 3Sum Extension
notes.description: This builds directly on the 3Sum two pointer pattern.

title: Sort Colors
description:
Given an array nums with n objects colored red, white, or blue, sort them in-place so that objects of the same color are adjacent.

The colors are represented by 0, 1, and 2.
hints: Maintain three regions: 0s, 1s, and 2s.
Use three pointers.
Move through the array once.
intuition: We divide the array into three sections: elements before low are zeros, between low and mid are ones, and after high are twos. By moving elements into their correct regions, we sort in one pass.

patternExplanation.name: Dutch National Flag Algorithm
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Use multiple pointers to divide an array into regions.

optimal.reason: Sort in a single traversal.

approaches.name: Dutch National Flag

pitfalls: Incrementing mid after swapping with high.

notes.title: Important Interview Pattern
notes.description: Dutch National Flag is a common Google/Amazon interview topic.

title: Maximum Average Subarray I
description:
You are given an integer array nums consisting of n elements and an integer k.

Find a contiguous subarray whose length is equal to k that has the maximum average value and return this value.

examples.explanation: The subarray [12,-5,-6,50] has the maximum average: (12-5-6+50)/4 = 12.75.

hints: Calculate the sum of the first k elements.
Move the window by removing the left element and adding the new right element.
Track the maximum window sum.
intuition: Instead of calculating the sum of every k-sized subarray separately, maintain one sliding window. When the window moves, subtract the outgoing element and add the incoming element.

patternExplanation.name: Fixed Size Sliding Window
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Maintain a window of fixed length and update it efficiently.

bruteForce.reason: Calculate sum again for every possible window.

optimal.reason: Each element enters and leaves the window once.

approaches.name: Fixed Sliding Window

edgeCases.reason: Maximum average can still be negative.

followUpQuestions: Find maximum sum of size k.

notes.title: Fixed Window Pattern
notes.description: Whenever window size is constant, sliding window avoids repeated calculations.

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
description: Given a string s, find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.

examples.explanation: The answer is "abc" with length 3.

constraints: s contains English letters, digits, symbols, and spaces
hints: Use two pointers to maintain current substring.
Store last seen position of each character.
Move left pointer when duplicate appears.
intuition: Maintain a window containing unique characters. When a duplicate character appears, move the left boundary forward until the window becomes valid again.

patternExplanation.name: Variable Size Sliding Window
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Expand the window when valid and shrink it when constraints break.

bruteForce.reason: Generate every substring and check duplicates.

optimal.reason: Each character is processed once using HashMap.

approaches.name: Sliding Window + HashMap

followUpQuestions: Longest substring with at most K distinct characters.

notes.title: Classic Sliding Window
notes.description: One of the most important string interview patterns.

title: Minimum Size Subarray Sum
description: Given an array of positive integers nums and a positive integer target, return the minimal length of a contiguous subarray whose sum is greater than or equal to target. If no such subarray exists, return 0.

examples.explanation: The subarray [4,3] has the smallest length with sum >= 7.

hints: Use two pointers to maintain a current window.
Expand the window until the sum reaches target.
Shrink the window to find the smallest length.
intuition: We keep expanding the right pointer to increase the sum. Once the sum becomes valid, we move the left pointer to remove unnecessary elements and minimize the window size.

patternExplanation.name: Variable Sliding Window
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Grow the window until the condition is satisfied, then shrink it to optimize the answer.

optimal.reason: Each element is added and removed from the window once.

approaches.name: Sliding Window

pitfalls: Using sliding window with negative numbers.
Forgetting to shrink after reaching target.
followUpQuestions: Find maximum length subarray with sum <= target.
Solve when negative numbers are allowed.

notes.title: Important Rule
notes.description: Classic sliding window works efficiently when numbers are positive.

title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
description:
You are given a string s and an integer k. You can choose any character of the string and change it to any other uppercase English character at most k times.

Return the length of the longest substring containing the same letter after performing at most k replacements.

examples.explanation: Replace two As with Bs or two Bs with As.

hints: Maintain frequency of characters inside the window.
Track the most frequent character count.
Window is valid when replacements needed <= k.
intuition: In a valid window, we keep the most frequent character unchanged and replace all other characters. If the number of replacements exceeds k, shrink the window.

patternExplanation.name: Frequency Based Sliding Window
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Maintain a window where the number of changes needed stays within the allowed limit.

optimal.reason: Each character is processed once.

approaches.name: Sliding Window + Frequency Array

edgeCases.reason: Need replacements to create a valid window.

notes.title: Advanced Sliding Window
notes.description: This pattern appears frequently in substring interview problems.

title: Permutation in String
description:
Given two strings s1 and s2, return true if s2 contains a permutation of s1, or false otherwise.

A permutation of a string means rearranging its characters to form another string.

examples.explanation: The substring "ba" is a permutation of "ab".

constraints: s1 and s2 contain lowercase English letters
hints: Create frequency count of s1.
Maintain a window of same size in s2.
Compare character frequencies.
intuition: A permutation has exactly the same character frequency. We maintain a fixed-size window in s2 equal to s1 length and check whether both frequency arrays match.

patternExplanation.name: Fixed Window Frequency Matching
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Keep a window of fixed size and compare character frequencies.

bruteForce.reason: Generate every substring and check permutation.

optimal.reason: Each character enters and leaves the window once.

approaches.name: Sliding Window Frequency

followUpQuestions: Solve with HashMap instead of array.

notes.title: Anagram Window Pattern
notes.description: Very common sliding window pattern for string matching.

title: Find All Anagrams in a String
description: Given two strings s and p, return an array of all start indices of p's anagrams in s.

examples.explanation: Substrings "cba" and "bac" are anagrams of "abc".

constraints: s and p contain lowercase English letters
hints: Window size should always equal pattern length.
Maintain character frequency.
Avoid sorting every substring.
intuition: Every anagram has the same character count. Instead of sorting every substring, maintain a frequency window and compare counts as the window moves.

patternExplanation.name: Fixed Size Anagram Window
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Move a fixed-size window and track character frequencies.

optimal.reason: Single sliding window traversal.

approaches.name: Sliding Window

notes.title: Interview Pattern
notes.description: A standard fixed sliding window problem.

title: Maximum Number of Vowels in a Substring of Given Length
description: Given a string s and an integer k, return the maximum number of vowel letters in any substring of s with length k.

examples.explanation: The substring "iii" contains 3 vowels.

constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: Maintain count of vowels in current window.
Add new character when expanding.
Remove old character when shrinking.
intuition: Since the window size is fixed, we only need to update the vowel count when one character enters and another leaves the window.

patternExplanation.name: Fixed Size Sliding Window
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Track only the changing part of the window instead of recalculating every substring.
whenToUse: Maximum/minimum values in k length window

bruteForce.reason: Count vowels separately for every substring.

optimal.reason: Each character is processed once.

approaches.name: Sliding Window

notes.title: Simple Window Pattern
notes.description: Useful starting problem for learning fixed sliding windows.

title: Longest Subarray of 1s After Deleting One Element
description: Given a binary array nums, delete one element from it and return the length of the longest non-empty subarray containing only 1s.

examples.explanation: Delete 0 and remaining longest sequence is [1,1,1].

hints: Allow at most one zero inside the window.
Count zeros while expanding.
Shrink when zeros exceed one.
intuition: We find the longest window containing at most one zero. Since one zero can be removed, the remaining window length is the answer minus one.

patternExplanation.name: At Most K Elements Window
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Maintain a window that violates the condition only after exceeding allowed changes.

optimal.reason: Single sliding window traversal.

approaches.name: Sliding Window

edgeCases.reason: Must delete one element, so length decreases by one.

followUpQuestions: Longest ones after flipping K zeros.

notes.title: Modification Window
notes.description: Same pattern as character replacement problems.

title: Max Consecutive Ones III
description: Given a binary array nums and an integer k, return the maximum number of consecutive 1s in the array if you can flip at most k zeros.

examples.explanation: Flip two zeros to get six consecutive ones.

hints: Maintain a window containing at most k zeros.
Expand the right pointer.
Shrink when zero count exceeds k.
intuition: Treat zeros as elements that can be changed. Keep a window where the number of zeros is at most k. The largest valid window is the answer.

patternExplanation.name: At Most K Changes Sliding Window
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Maintain the largest window satisfying a limit condition.

optimal.reason: Each element enters and leaves the window once.

approaches.name: Sliding Window

pitfalls: Counting ones instead of invalid elements.
followUpQuestions: Return starting index of longest window.

notes.title: Same Pattern Family
notes.description: This is the same idea as Longest Repeating Character Replacement.

title: Fruit Into Baskets
description:
You are given an array fruits where fruits[i] represents the type of fruit at position i.

You have two baskets and each basket can hold only one type of fruit. Find the length of the longest contiguous subarray containing at most two different fruit types.

examples.explanation: The longest valid subarray is [1,2,2].

hints: Maintain frequency of fruit types inside window.
Window can contain maximum two unique values.
Remove elements from left when unique count exceeds two.
intuition: This is a longest substring problem where the condition is maximum two unique values. Use a HashMap to track frequencies and shrink the window when a third type appears.

patternExplanation.name: Longest Window With K Distinct Elements
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Maintain a valid window using frequency counting.
whenToUse: Longest substring with K distinct values

bruteForce.reason: Generate every subarray and count types.

optimal.reason: HashMap stores only active window elements.

approaches.name: Sliding Window + HashMap

edgeCases.reason: Window shrinks to maintain two types.

pitfalls: Tracking only unique count without frequency.
followUpQuestions: Find longest window with K fruit types.

notes.title: K Distinct Pattern
notes.description: Very common sliding window template.

title: Running Sum of 1d Array
description: Given an array nums, return the running sum of nums where runningSum[i] = nums[0] + nums[1] + ... + nums[i].

examples.explanation: Each element stores the sum of all previous elements including itself.

hints: Current prefix sum depends on previous prefix sum.
Store cumulative value while traversing.
intuition: Instead of calculating the sum again for every index, keep adding the current number to the previous sum.

patternExplanation.name: Basic Prefix Sum
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Store cumulative information while moving from left to right.

bruteForce.reason: Calculate sum from beginning for every index.

optimal.reason: Each element is processed once.

approaches.name: Prefix Sum

edgeCases.reason: Prefix sum works with any integer values.

pitfalls: Confusing prefix sum with normal sum.
followUpQuestions: Find range sum between two indices.
Build prefix sum without modifying original array.

notes.title: Foundation Problem
notes.description: This is the first step before solving advanced prefix sum questions.

title: Find Pivot Index
description: Given an array nums, return the leftmost index where the sum of all numbers strictly to the left is equal to the sum of all numbers strictly to the right.

examples.explanation: Left sum = 11 and right sum = 11.

hints: Calculate total sum first.
Maintain left sum while traversing.
Right sum can be calculated using total sum.
intuition: At every index, right sum = total sum - left sum - current element. Compare left and right sums.

patternExplanation.name: Left Right Prefix Sum
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Use total sum to avoid calculating right side repeatedly.

bruteForce.reason: Calculate left and right sum for every index.

optimal.reason: Maintain running left sum.

approaches.name: Prefix Sum Optimization

pitfalls: Including current element in left or right sum.

notes.title: Important Pattern
notes.description: Frequently used before advanced subarray sum problems.

title: Range Sum Query - Immutable
description:
Given an integer array nums, handle multiple queries of the following type:

Calculate the sum of the elements of nums between indices left and right inclusive.

examples.explanation: Each query returns the sum between the given indexes.

hints: Multiple queries should not recalculate sums.
Create a prefix sum array once.
Range sum = prefix[right] - prefix[left-1].
intuition: If we calculate every range sum separately, many values are recalculated. Prefix sum stores previous calculations so every query becomes an O(1) operation.

patternExplanation.name: Prefix Sum for Range Queries
patternExplanation.coreIdea: Precompute cumulative sums to answer future range queries quickly.

bruteForce.reason: Traverse every element inside the range.

optimal.reason: Prefix array stores previous sums.

approaches.name: Prefix Sum Array

pitfalls: Forgetting extra size in prefix array.
followUpQuestions: How to handle updates in array?
Can prefix sum work in 2D arrays?
Difference between Prefix Sum and Fenwick Tree?

notes.title: Important Interview Pattern
notes.description: Foundation for many subarray sum problems.

title: Subarray Sum Equals K
description: Given an array of integers nums and an integer k, return the total number of subarrays whose sum equals k.

examples.explanation: The subarrays [1,1] and [1,1] have sum 2.

title: Continuous Subarray Sum
description:
Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return true if nums has a good subarray.

A good subarray is a subarray where:

- The sum of its elements is a multiple of k.

hints: Store prefix sum remainder.
If the same remainder appears again, the middle elements sum to multiple of k.
Store first occurrence of each remainder.
intuition: If two prefix sums have the same remainder after dividing by k, their difference is divisible by k. The elements between those two positions form a valid subarray.
